rules.reference: Superior authority cannot exercise powers denied to subordinate authority
rules.relevance: The court ruled that the Custodian General cannot do something which the Custodian or District Judge could not have done or was prohibited from doing.
The court examined whether the allottee's interest was capable of acquisition and disposal, a requirement for protection under this article.
The court considered whether the cancellation amounted to deprivation of property without authority of law.
The court analyzed whether the cancellation constituted acquisition or requisitioning requiring compensation.
This section empowers the Custodian to vary or cancel allotments, establishing the provisional nature of the allottee's rights.

rules.case_name: H. D. Vora vs State of Maharashtra and Ors.
rules.reference: H. D. Vora vs State of Maharashtra and Ors.
rules.relevance: Established that an order of requisition is by its nature temporary and cannot continue for an indefinite period; otherwise, it amounts to a fraud on the statute and a misuse of power.

rules.case_name: Collector of Akola and Ors. vs Ramachandra & Ors.
rules.reference: Collector of Akola and Ors. vs Ramachandra & Ors.
rules.relevance: Held that an order of requisition can be made for a permanent public purpose, distinguishing the validity of the initial order from the duration of its continuance.
Discussed to determine if the government had the power to acquire part of a building, which is relevant to whether requisition was a misuse of power when acquisition was possible.

Requisition involves taking possession for a limited period, whereas acquisition involves transfer of title; using requisition for permanent purposes when acquisition is possible is a misuse of power.

rules.reference: West Bengal Premises Requisition and Control (Temporary Provision) Act, 1947
rules.relevance: The statute under which the premises were requisitioned and which is the subject of the challenge regarding its temporary nature.
The court interpreted this provision to determine if the Municipal Corporation had the statutory power to grant a license for the subsoil of a park for an underground market.

rules.case_name: Attorney General vs Corporation of Sunderland
rules.reference: Attorney General vs Corporation of Sunderland
rules.relevance: The court distinguished this case to reject the argument that the Corporation acts as a trustee and cannot use park land for purposes other than those strictly contemplated, noting the intrinsic character of the park was preserved.

rules.reference: Intrinsic character of a public park
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that development work is permissible provided it does not destroy the intrinsic character of the park as a place of public recreation.
The court invoked the principle of public interest to direct a revision of the license fee and terms, ensuring they were not detrimental to the public despite the statutory validity of the grant.
The statutory framework under which the applicants sought to commit the respondents for contempt.
Requires the trial court to examine the accused regarding material circumstances appearing against him.
The provision under which the appellant was convicted for culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
Defines the High Court's power to review evidence and set aside an order of acquittal.

rules.reference: Presumption of innocence reinforced by acquittal
rules.relevance: An order of acquittal reinforces the presumption of innocence; it can only be reversed for very substantial and compelling reasons, not merely because the accused failed to explain circumstances.

rules.case_name: Tara Singh vs The State
rules.relevance: Establishes that the object of Section 342 CrPC is to afford a fair opportunity to explain circumstances, and that errors in compliance are curable irregularities if no prejudice is caused.
Procedural errors do not necessarily vitiate a trial; the test is whether the error caused prejudice to the accused.
Establishes that an accomplice is a competent witness and a conviction is not illegal merely because it proceeds upon uncorroborated testimony.
The court applied the principle that each circumstance must be established beyond doubt and all circumstances together must lead to the only inference of guilt.
Postulates that an accomplice is unworthy of credit unless corroborated in material particulars.
The court considered that an extra-judicial confession made after a long lapse of time, where one witness retracts, cannot be relied upon.

This section provides relief from double taxation when a person carrying on a business is succeeded by another. It explicitly states that a 'mere change in the constitution of a partnership' does not amount to succession for the purposes of this relief.
The charging section establishes that a firm is a distinct assessable entity separate from its individual partners for income tax purposes.

These provisions support the position that the technical view of partnership under general law (where a firm has no legal existence apart from partners) cannot be strictly applied to income tax assessment.

The court established that the true question is the identity of the unit assessed under the Income-tax Act. A firm retains its identity as an assessable unit despite changes in partners, provided there is no dissolution or division of assets.
The court determined that this section applies only to cases of discontinuance of business, not mere dissolution or reconstitution where business continues.
The statutory provision governing the registration of partnership firms for tax purposes.
These sections govern assessment in cases of change in constitution or succession to business, recognizing the firm as a unit of assessment independent of partners.
The provision authorizing the imposition of penalty for concealment of income, applicable to 'persons' including firms.
Limits the scope of a reference to the High Court to questions that were raised or argued before the Tribunal.
The central provision requiring a firm to be 'constituted under an instrument of partnership' to be eligible for registration.
The court held that Section 104 applies to the original side of the High Court and provides an additional remedy for appeals against orders, without overriding the Letters Patent.
The court determined that Order 43 Rule 1 applies to proceedings before a Trial Judge of the High Court, making orders listed therein appealable to a larger Bench.

rules.reference: Letters Patent of the Bombay High Court
rules.relevance: The central issue was interpreting the word 'judgment' in Clause 15 to determine the maintainability of appeals from a Single Judge to a Division Bench.
The court used Section 4 to establish that the Code does not limit or affect special laws like the Letters Patent, but rather supplements them.
The court relied on Section 117 to confirm that the provisions of the Code apply to High Courts unless expressly excluded.
The court noted that Order 49 Rule 3 exempts certain rules from applying to Chartered High Courts but does not exempt Order 43 Rule 1, implying its applicability.

rules.case_name: Hurrish Chunder Chowdry v. Kali Sundari Debia
rules.reference: Hurrish Chunder Chowdry v. Kali Sundari Debia
rules.relevance: The Privy Council held that Section 588 of the 1877 Code (predecessor to Order 43) did not restrict appeals under the Letters Patent, supporting the view that Code provisions apply to internal High Court appeals.

rules.case_name: Mt. Sabitri Thakurain v. Savi
rules.relevance: The Privy Council held that regulations under the Code apply to jurisdiction exercisable under the Letters Patent, except where they restrict express Letters Patent appeals.

rules.case_name: Union of India v. Mohindra Supply Co.
rules.reference: Union of India v. Mohindra Supply Co.
rules.relevance: The Supreme Court held that Section 104 preserves the right to appeal conferred by other laws, including the Letters Patent, and does not affect it.

rules.case_name: Shankarlal Aggarwal v. Shankarlal Poddar
rules.relevance: The Supreme Court observed that the expression 'judgment' in Clause 15 is wider than appealable orders under Section 104/Order 43, and that Section 104 does not override the Letters Patent.

rules.reference: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: The court held that this section, providing benefits during pendency, was inapplicable because the Act itself did not apply to the building due to the Section 2(2) exemption.

rules.reference: U.P. Rent Control and Eviction Act
rules.relevance: This section exempts buildings constructed on or after January 1, 1951, from the Act. The court examined whether this exemption was a mandatory public policy restriction or a benefit that could be waived by the landlord.

rules.reference: U.P. Rent Control and Eviction Act
rules.relevance: This section imposes restrictions on eviction. The appellant sought protection under this section, contingent on the validity of the waiver of Section 1A.
The court analyzed whether the agreement to waive Section 1A had an unlawful object or defeated the provisions of any law, rendering it void.

rules.reference: Cuilibet licet renuntiare juri pro se introducto
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that an individual may waive a statutory right conferred for their private benefit, provided it does not infringe public policy or public rights.

rules.case_name: Neminath Appayya Hanumannavar vs Jamboorao Satappa Kocheri
rules.reference: Neminath Appayya Hanumannavar vs Jamboorao Satappa Kocheri
rules.relevance: The court relied on this precedent to interpret Section 23 of the Contract Act, establishing that an agreement defeats the law only if its performance necessarily entails the transgression of that law.

rules.case_name: Vita Food Products Incorporated vs Unus Company Ltd.
rules.reference: Vita Food Products Incorporated vs Unus Company Ltd.
rules.relevance: The court referred to Lord Wright's observations that contracts should not be nullified for disobedience to statute unless serious public policy grounds exist.

rules.case_name: Ram Saroop Rai vs Lilavati
rules.relevance: The court relied on this decision to support the view that the Act applies based on the explicit language of Section 2(2), distinguishing it from earlier conflicting authority.

rules.reference: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: Exempts buildings from the Act for ten years from the date construction is completed. The court interpreted whether this exemption persists if the ten-year period expires during litigation.

rules.reference: U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972
rules.relevance: The court interpreted this provision to determine that the Act exempts buildings for ten years from completion, and that for assessed buildings, the date of first assessment is the deemed date of completion.

Provides for penalty and recovery of property wrongfully obtained or withheld by an officer or employee of a company. The court interpreted this to include former employees who withhold property after termination.
The provision under which the High Court exercised its inherent powers to quash the proceedings. The Supreme Court reviewed whether this power was exercised correctly.
Considered to determine if any irregularity in the filing of the complaint was curable.

rules.case_name: Baldev Krishna Sahi vs Shipping Corpn. of India Ltd.
rules.reference: Baldev Krishna Sahi vs Shipping Corpn. of India Ltd.
rules.relevance: Established that Section 630 applies to past officers or employees who wrongfully withhold company property after the termination of their employment.

rules.case_name: Damodar Das Jain vs Krishna Charan Chakraborti
rules.reference: Damodar Das Jain vs Krishna Charan Chakraborti
rules.relevance: Held that criminal courts should not adjudicate if there is a bona fide dispute regarding title. The Supreme Court distinguished this case on facts, finding no bona fide dispute here.
A dispute is not 'bona fide' if it is fabricated by an employee through self-serving documents or if the employee's claim contradicts their own prior admissions and the primary agreement.

rules.reference: Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949

rules.reference: Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949
rules.relevance: Provides that if no allotment order is passed within 15 days of intimation of vacancy, the landlord is free to let the house to any person.

rules.reference: Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949
rules.relevance: Mandates that a tenant allotted premises under Clause 23 or 24A must vacate upon ceasing to hold an office of profit.

rules.reference: Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949
rules.relevance: Confers power on the Collector to take steps to secure compliance with the Order, including eviction for contravention.

Defines 'agricultural income' as rent or revenue derived from land used for agricultural purposes that is either assessed to land revenue or subject to a local rate. The case hinges on the interpretation of 'assessed to land revenue'.
Provides exemption for agricultural income. The applicability of this exemption depends on the definition in Section 2(1)(a).
Governs the acquisition of land for public purposes. The court analyzed this to determine if acquisition alone extinguished land revenue assessment.

rules.reference: Effect of Redemption of Land Revenue
rules.relevance: The court established that a lump sum payment equal to the capitalized value of land revenue extinguishes the assessment in perpetuity, rendering the land 'revenue free'.
Authorized the redemption of existing land revenue by immediate payment of a sum equal in value to the revenue redeemed, confirming the government's intent to extinguish the recurring demand.

rules.reference: The Land Law of Bengal (Tagore Law Lectures, 1895)
rules.relevance: Cited to support the classification of lands granted proprietary title free from land revenue in consideration of a capitalized sum as 'revenue free' lands.
The court held that the operative clause of the conveyance deed, which discharged the land from all land revenue, was clear and unambiguous, confirming the extinction of the assessment.
The court interpreted the terms 'accrue' or 'arise' to determine when compensation income becomes taxable.

rules.reference: Kedarnath Jute Mfg. Co. Limited. vs Commissioner of Income Tax (Central), Calcutta
rules.relevance: Distinguished because in that case liability arose immediately and only quantification remained, whereas here the right to payment was in dispute.

The court applied the principle that the accession of one State to another is an 'act of State', and a successor State does not automatically inherit the contractual obligations of a merged State unless it recognizes them.

rules.case_name: Secretary of State in Council of India v. Kamachee Boye Saheba
rules.reference: Secretary of State in Council of India v. Kamachee Boye Saheba

rules.relevance: Cited for the principle that inhabitants of acquired territory can only enforce rights recognized by the new sovereign in municipal courts.

rules.reference: Rajasthan (Regulation of Customs Duties) Ordinance No. 16 of 1949
rules.relevance: The court held that this Ordinance repealed previous customs laws and introduced a new uniform tariff, thereby superseding any previous contractual rights regarding customs concessions.

rules.reference: Article 295 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: The court held that Article 295 does not prohibit Parliament or State Legislatures from enacting laws that alter the terms and conditions of contracts or grants made by former rulers.

rules.reference: Article 306 of the Constitution of India
rules.relevance: The court held that Article 306, which allows Part B States to continue levying certain taxes, is inapplicable to claims based on private contractual liability rather than statutory levy.
The court affirmed that State Legislatures have plenary power to enact laws altering previous contracts or grants unless expressly prohibited by the Constitution.

Article 286(1)(a) prohibits States from taxing sales taking place 'outside the State'. The Explanation deems a sale to take place in the State where goods are delivered for the purpose of consumption in that State, creating a legal fiction for determining the situs of the sale.

Section 2(g) defined 'sale' based on territorial nexus (e.g., goods present in Bihar at contract). Section 33 incorporated the restrictions of Article 286 into the Act, limiting the State's taxing power.

rules.case_name: The State of Bombay v. United Motors (India) Ltd.
rules.reference: The State of Bombay v. United Motors (India) Ltd.
rules.relevance: Established that the Explanation to Article 286(1)(a) defines 'inside' sales; sales satisfying the Explanation are taxable only in the State of delivery for consumption and are 'outside' all other States.

The court identified three fundamental principles: minimum wage (mandatory), fair wage (related to earning capacity and workload), and living wage (the goal). Revision is necessary when fair wages sag due to rising prices.

rules.case_name: Greaves Cotton & Co. vs Their Workmen
rules.relevance: The court applied the principle that if few comparable industries exist in a region, the 'region' part of the formula assumes importance to prevent unfair competition and industrial unrest.
The court considered the employer's financial capacity, noting that the burden of increased wages must be assessable against profits and sales.

rules.case_name: Novex Dry Cleaners vs Its Workmen
rules.reference: Novex Dry Cleaners vs Its Workmen
rules.relevance: The court clarified that guidelines regarding comparative profit studies are not rigid statutory enactments but flexible inquiries dependent on the facts of each case.

rules.case_name: Hindustan Times, Ltd. vs Their Workmen
rules.reference: Hindustan Times, Ltd. vs Their Workmen
rules.relevance: The court relied on this case to justify departing from point-to-point adjustment in favor of granting increments based on service length to provide relief to existing employees.
An appeal by special leave is not an appeal as of right; interference is limited to cases of excess of jurisdiction, substantial error in law, or gross palpable error.

Defines 'workman' and excludes supervisory staff drawing wages exceeding Rs. 500 per month, which is central to determining the Tribunal's jurisdiction.
Defines 'industrial dispute', relevant to determining if a dispute survives when the persons involved cease to be 'workmen'.

rules.case_name: All India Reserve Bank of India Employees Association vs Reserve Bank of India
rules.reference: All India Reserve Bank of India Employees Association vs Reserve Bank of India
rules.relevance: Established that supervisory staff drawing less than Rs. 500 cannot be debarred from claiming wages exceeding Rs. 500, and that the Tribunal retains jurisdiction if workmen exist at the time of reference, even if they become non-workmen later.
Defines the scope of disputes touching the constitution, management, or business of a society that must be referred to the Registrar.
Bars civil courts from entertaining suits regarding disputes referred to the Registrar under Section 91(1).
Excludes civil court jurisdiction over disputes required to be referred to the Registrar or his nominee.

rules.case_name: Deccan Merchants Co-operative Bank Ltd. vs M/s Dalichand Jugraj Jain and others
rules.reference: Deccan Merchants Co-operative Bank Ltd. vs M/s Dalichand Jugraj Jain and others
rules.relevance: Established that the Bombay Rent Act and the Co-operative Societies Act should be harmonized, with the Rent Act applying to matters covered by it.
Establishes that a licence granted for a limited period is deemed revoked upon the expiry of that period.

rules.reference: The Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
rules.relevance: Defines 'licensee' as a person in occupation under a 'subsisting agreement for licence'.

rules.reference: The Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947
rules.relevance: Confers tenant status on a licensee who is in occupation under a subsisting agreement on February 1, 1973.

Filing an application for eviction under Section 41 does not imply a grant of a fresh licence or revive an expired one.
Defines 'charitable purpose' to include the advancement of any other object of general public utility, provided it is not involving the carrying on of any activity for profit.
Provides exemption from tax for income derived from property held under trust or legal obligation for charitable or religious purposes.

rules.case_name: Additional Commissioner of Income Tax, Gujarat vs Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers' Association
rules.reference: Additional Commissioner of Income Tax, Gujarat vs Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers' Association
rules.relevance: Established the 'doctrine of dominant or primary object', holding that if the primary object is charitable, incidental profit-making activities do not disqualify the trust from exemption.

rules.reference: Doctrine of Dominant or Primary Object
rules.relevance: Determines that the character of the trust is defined by its main object; ancillary activities generating profit do not negate charitable status if profit is not the real object.
Distinguishes between the charitable purpose of a trust and the powers conferred on trustees (e.g., employee benefits) which are incidental to the proper functioning of the organization.
Excludes from total income any income derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable purposes.

rules.case_name: Loka Shikshana Trust vs C.I.T., Mysore
rules.reference: Loka Shikshana Trust vs C.I.T., Mysore
rules.relevance: Established that for a purpose to be charitable under Section 2(15), it must be shown that the advancement of the object does not involve carrying on any activity for profit.

rules.case_name: C.I.T. vs. Andhra Chamber of Commerce
rules.reference: C.I.T. vs. Andhra Chamber of Commerce

An activity is presumed to be for profit if it is ordinarily carried on by private entities for gain, unless there is a built-in restriction in the constitution or practice negating the profit motive.

Empowers State Transport Authority to grant regular All India Tourist Permits. The court noted the deliberate omission of Section 62 from the list of sections applicable to these permits, indicating legislative intent to exclude temporary permits.

Authorizes the State transport undertaking to prepare a scheme for road transport services in any area, route, or portion thereof.

Requires consideration of applicant's experience, financial soundness, and technical knowledge, establishing the personal nature of the qualification.

rules.case_name: Banarsi Das vs Cane Commissioner, U.P.

rules.relevance: Established that conditions similar to Rule 27 are directory, not mandatory.

Used to determine that teaching experience from foreign institutions recognized under these sections is valid.
